blocks.translation: Voluntary prayer is disliked after the rising of dawn beyond its sunnah, after the dawn prayer itself, after the Asr prayer, before Maghrib, when the preacher comes out until he finishes the prayer, at the time of the iqamah—except for the sunnah of Fajr—before the Eid prayer even at home and after it in the mosque, between the two combined prayers at Arafah and Muzdalifah, when the time of the obligatory prayer is narrow, when resisting the two impurities (the call of nature), when food is present that one's soul craves, and whatever preoccupies the mind and disturbs khushu‘.

The adhan and iqamah are established as an emphasized sunnah for the obligatory prayers—even when prayed alone, whether performed on time or made up, in travel or residence—for men; and they are disliked for women.
He says the takbir four times at the beginning, repeats the takbir at the end twice like the rest of its phrases, and there is no tarji‘ (silent repetition) of the two testimonies.
And the iqamah is like it.

He adds, after "falah" in the Fajr adhan, "al-salatu khayrun mina al-nawm" (prayer is better than sleep) twice, and after "falah" in the iqamah, "qad qamati al-salah" (the prayer has been established) twice.
He proceeds slowly in the adhan and hastens in the iqamah.
It does not suffice in Persian even if it is known to be an adhan, according to the most correct opinion.

It is recommended that the muezzin be righteous, knowledgeable of the sunnah and the times of prayer, in a state of wudu, facing the qiblah—unless he is riding—and that he place his two fingers in his two ears.
He turns his face to the right at 'come to prayer' and to the left at 'come to success', and he turns around within his minaret.

He separates between the adhan and the iqama by the amount of time it takes for the regular attendants to arrive for the prayer, while observing the recommended time; and in Maghrib by a pause equal to reciting three short verses or three steps.
And he performs tathwib, such as saying after the adhan: 'The prayer, the prayer, O worshippers!'

Disliked are: melodic intoning of the adhan; the iqama of one in minor impurity and his adhan; the adhan of one in major impurity, of an uncomprehending boy, of a madman, a drunkard, a woman, a sinner, or one sitting; and speech during the adhan and iqama — and it is recommended to repeat it (the adhan) but not the iqama.
Both (adhan and iqama) are disliked for the Dhuhr prayer on Friday within the city.

He gives the adhan and iqama for a missed prayer, and likewise for the first of several missed prayers; it is disliked to omit the iqama — though not the adhan — for the remaining missed prayers if the sitting of make-up is the same.

When the listener hears the sunnah call from him (the muezzin), he refrains from recitation and repeats the like of what he says, and says the hawqala at the two hay'alas, and says 'You have spoken the truth and acted righteously' or 'Whatever Allah wills' at the muezzin's words 'Prayer is better than sleep'; then he supplicates with the wasila for the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him), saying: 'O Allah, Lord of this perfect call and established prayer, grant Muhammad the wasila and the eminence, and raise him to the praiseworthy station which You promised him.'

blocks.en: Chapter on the Conditions of the Prayer and its Integrals

blocks.translation: The validity of the prayer requires twenty-seven things:
Purification from ritual impurity (ḥadath).
Purity of the body, the garment, and the place from non-excused filth — even the spot of the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, and the forehead, according to the more correct view.
Covering of the nakedness — though seeing it through his collar or from the bottom of his hem does not invalidate it.

Facing the qiblah: for the Meccan who sees the Kaʿbah his obligation is to face its very substance; for one not seeing it — even in Mecca, according to the correct view — facing its direction suffices.
The (entry of the) time.
Believing that the time has entered.
The intention.
The taḥrīmah (opening takbīr) without anything separating it (from the intention).
Performing the taḥrīmah while standing, before bending down for the rukūʿ.
Not delaying the intention until after the taḥrīmah.
Pronouncing the taḥrīmah audibly enough that he hears himself, according to the more correct view.
The follower's intention to follow (the imām).
Specifying the obligatory prayer.
And of the obligatory prayer — not the supererogatory —,
And standing in other than the supererogatory prayer,

And the recitation — even of a single verse — in the two rakʿahs of the obligatory prayer and in all of the supererogatory and the witr; no specific portion of the Qur'an is specified for the validity of the prayer; the follower does not recite, but rather listens and remains silent, and if he does recite it is disliked with a prohibitive dislike.
And the bowing,

And the prostration upon something whose solidity he can feel and upon which his forehead rests firmly — even on his palm or the edge of his garment, provided the place of its placing is pure — and he prostrates on the hard part of his nose along with his forehead; restricting it to the nose alone is not valid according to the most correct view, except in the case of an excuse affecting the forehead,

And that the place of prostration not be raised above the place of the two feet by more than half a cubit — and if it exceeds half a cubit it is not permitted, except in the case of a crowd in which he prostrates upon the back of someone praying the same prayer —,

And the placing of the two hands and the two knees — according to the sound view — and of something of the toes of the two feet upon the ground during the prostration; placing the top of the foot does not suffice —,
And the performing of the bowing before the prostration,
And the rising from prostration to a position close to sitting, according to the most correct view,
And the returning to prostration,
And the final sitting for the duration of the tashahhud,
[25] And delaying it (the intention) from the pillars.
[26] And performing them while awake.

[27] And knowing the manner of the prayer and what it contains of obligatory elements in a way that distinguishes them from the sunnah elements, or believing that all of them are obligatory, so that he does not perform a supererogatory act in place of an obligatory one.
The pillars among the items mentioned are four:
[1] Standing,
[2] And recitation,
[3] And bowing,
[4] And prostration.
And it is said: the final sitting for the duration of the tashahhud (is also a pillar).
The rest of them are conditions: some are conditions for the validity of commencing the prayer—namely those external to it—while others are conditions for the continued validity of the prayer.

Prayer is permissible upon a felt mat whose upper face is pure while the lower is impure; and upon a pure garment whose lining is impure, provided it is not quilted; and upon a pure end (of a cloth), even if the impure end moves with the movement of the one praying, according to the sound view.
If one of the two ends of his turban becomes impure, and he throws it off keeping the pure end on his head, and the impure end does not move with his movement, then his prayer is valid;
But if it does move…
it is not permissible.
One who lacks the means to remove impurity prays with it and need not repeat the prayer.
Nor is repetition required upon one who lacks something to cover his nakedness — even if it be silk, grass, or clay.
If he finds it — even by way of loan — and a quarter of it is pure, his prayer naked is not valid.
He is given a choice if less than a quarter of it is pure, and his praying with it while all of it is impure is more preferable than praying naked.
If he finds something that covers part of the nakedness, its use is obligatory, and he covers the front and the rear.
If it only covers one of them, it is said he covers the rear, and it is said the front.
The prayer of the naked one is recommended to be performed sitting by gesture, stretching his legs toward the qibla.
If he prays standing by gesture, or with bowing and prostration, it is valid.
The nakedness of the man is what is between the navel and the end of the knee.
The female slave adds to that the belly and the back.
The entire body of the free woman is nakedness except her face, hands, and feet.
The exposure of a quarter of one of the limbs of nakedness prevents the validity of the prayer.
If the exposure is scattered over several limbs of nakedness, and the total of what is exposed reaches a quarter of the smallest of the exposed limbs, it invalidates; otherwise, no.
Whoever is unable to face the qibla due to illness, or is unable to dismount from his mount, or fears an enemy, his qibla is the direction of his ability and safety.
Whoever is uncertain about the qibla, and has no informer nor prayer niche, exercises his judgment.
And there is no repetition upon him if he erred.
If he learns of his mistake during his prayer, he turns and continues upon what he has done.
And if he begins…

If he prays without making an effort to determine the direction and then, after finishing, learns that he indeed faced the qiblah, his prayer is valid; but if he learned during the prayer that he was facing it correctly, it is invalidated — just as it would be if he never knew whether he had faced it at all.
If a group of people each made an effort to determine different directions and did not know which direction their imam faced, their prayer suffices them.

blocks.en: Section: On the Obligatory Acts (Wajibat) of the Prayer

blocks.translation: They are eighteen things:
Reciting al-Fatihah,
Joining a surah or three verses in two unspecified rakʿahs of the obligatory prayer, and in all rakʿahs of the witr and the supererogatory prayer,
Designating the recitation to be in the first two rakʿahs of the obligatory prayer,
Giving precedence to al-Fatihah over the surah,
Placing the nose along with the forehead in the prostration,
Performing the second prostration in every rakʿah before moving on to anything else,
Tranquility (ṭumaʾnīnah) in the pillars,
The first sitting,
Reciting the tashahhud in it — according to the sound view —
And his reciting [the tashahhud] in the final sitting,
And rising to the third [rak'ah] without delay after the tashahhud,
And pronouncing the salam — without 'alaykum —,
And the qunut of the witr,
And the takbirs of the two Eids,
And specifying the takbir for the opening of every prayer — not the two Eid prayers specifically —,
And the takbir of the ruku' in the second [rak'ah] of the two Eids,
And the imam's reciting aloud in the recitation of Fajr and the first two [rak'ahs] of the two 'isha prayers — even if as makeup —, and of Jumu'ah, the two Eids, the Tarawih, and the witr in Ramadan,

And reciting silently in Zuhr, Asr, what comes after the first two [rak'ahs] of the two 'isha prayers, and the daytime supererogatory prayers; while the one praying alone has a choice in what he recites aloud, like one performing nafl at night.
And if he omits the surah in the first two [rak'ahs] of the 'isha, he recites it in the last two along with the Fatihah aloud; and if he omits the Fatihah, he does not repeat it in the last two.
And they are fifty-one:
Raising the two hands for the takbir of consecration to the level of the ears for the man and the slave-woman, and to the level of the shoulders for the free woman,
And spreading the fingers,
And the follower's opening takbir coinciding with that of his imam.

And the man's placing of his right hand upon his left below his navel — the manner of placement being that he places the inside of his right palm on the back of his left palm, encircling the wrist with his little finger and thumb.
And the woman's placing of her two hands upon her chest without encircling.
And the opening laudation (thanā').
And seeking refuge (ta'awwudh) for the recitation.
And the basmala at the beginning of every rak'ah.
And saying āmīn.
And the taḥmīd (saying rabbanā lakal-ḥamd).
And saying them (the basmala, ta'awwudh, āmīn, and taḥmīd) silently.
And standing erect at the opening takbir without lowering the head.
And the imam's saying aloud the takbir and the tasmī' (sami'a Allahu liman ḥamidah).
And spacing the two feet during the standing by the measure of four fingers.
And that the surah joined to al-Fātiḥah be from the long mufaṣṣal in Fajr and Ẓuhr, from its middle ones in 'Aṣr and 'Ishā', and from its short ones in Maghrib — if he is a resident.
And whichever sura he wishes, if he is a traveler,
And lengthening the first [rakʿah] in the Fajr prayer only,
And the takbir of the rukūʿ,
And its tasbīḥ three times,
And grasping his two knees with his two hands,
And spreading his fingers — but the woman does not spread them —
And keeping his shins erect,
And flattening his back,
And keeping his head level with his rear,
And rising from the rukūʿ,
And standing tranquilly after it,
And placing his knees, then his hands, then his face for the prostration,
And the reverse of that for rising up,
And the takbir of the prostration,
And the takbir of rising from it,
And the prostration being between his two palms,
And its tasbīḥ three times,
And the man keeping his belly away from his thighs, his elbows from his sides, and his forearms off the ground.
And the woman lowering herself and pressing her belly against her thighs.
And the rising to stand (after bowing).
And the sitting between the two prostrations.
And placing the hands upon the thighs between the two prostrations, as in the position of the tashahhud.
And spreading out his left leg and setting up the right (during sitting).
And the woman's sitting upon her left hip (tawarruk).
And, according to the sound view, pointing with the index finger at the shahadah: raising it at the negation and lowering it at the affirmation.
And the recitation of al-Fatihah in the rakʿahs after the first two.
And invoking blessings upon the Prophet (Allah bless him and grant him peace) in the final sitting.
And supplication with words resembling the expressions of the Qur'an and Sunnah, not the speech of people.
And turning to the right then to the left with the two salams.
And the imam intending — by the two salams — the men, the guardian angels, and the righteous of the jinn, according to the more correct view.
And the follower intending his imam in his direction; and if he is aligned with him, he intends him in both salams together with the congregation, the recording angels, and the righteous of the jinn.
And the one praying alone intending only the angels.
And lowering the voice in the second salam below the first.
And his giving the salam simultaneously with the imam's salam.
And beginning with the right side.
And the latecomer's waiting for the imam to finish.

Among its etiquettes are: the man's bringing his palms out from his sleeves at the takbir; the worshipper looking at the place of his prostration while standing, at the tops of his feet while bowing, at the tip of his nose while prostrating, at his lap while sitting, and at his shoulders while making the salam; warding off coughing as much as he can; covering his mouth at yawning; standing when 'Hayya 'ala al-falah' is said; and the imam's commencing the prayer when 'Qad qamati al-salah' is said.

blocks.en: On the manner of performing the prayer

blocks.translation: When he intends to enter the prayer, he brings his palms out from his sleeves, then raises them level with his ears, then says the takbir without elongation, having formed the intention.

Commencing the prayer is valid with any remembrance done purely for Allah Most High, such as 'Subhan Allah,' and in Persian if one is unable to use Arabic—just as one unable to use Arabic may recite in Persian; but if he is able to use Arabic, then according to the soundest view neither his commencing nor his reciting in Persian is valid.

Then he places his right hand on his left below his navel immediately after the takbir of consecration without delay, reciting the opening supplication, which is: 'Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no deity besides You.' Every worshipper recites this opening.
Then he silently seeks refuge for the recitation: the latecomer performs it but not the follower, and it is delayed past the takbirs of the two Eids.

Then he says the basmala silently—and he says it in every rakʿah before the Fatihah only—then recites the Fatihah, and the imam and the follower say amin silently; then he recites a surah or three verses.

Then he said the takbir while bowing calmly, leveling his head with his hindquarters, grasping his knees with his hands and spreading his fingers, and he glorified [Allah] in it three times, which is its minimum.

Then he raised his head and was still, saying: 'Allah has heard whoever praises Him; our Lord, to You is the praise,' if he is an imam or praying alone; and the follower suffices with the tahmid (saying 'rabbana laka l-hamd').

Then he said the takbir going down for prostration; he placed his knees, then his hands, then his face between his palms, and prostrated on his nose and forehead calmly, glorifying [Allah] three times, which is its minimum; and he separated his belly from his thighs and his upper arms from his armpits, when not crowded, directing the fingers of his hands and his feet toward the qiblah; the woman, however, lowers herself and presses her belly against her thighs.
Then he raised his head saying takbir and sat between the two prostrations, placing his hands on his thighs calmly.
Then he said the takbir and prostrated calmly, glorifying [Allah] in it three times, separating his belly from his thighs and exposing his upper arms.
Then he raised his head saying takbir to stand up, without leaning on the ground with his hands and without sitting.
And the second rakʿah is like the first, except that he does not recite the opening praise (thana') nor the taʿawwudh.

Raising the hands is not sunnah except at the opening of every prayer, at the takbir of the qunut in witr, at the additional takbirs in the two Eid prayers, when he sees the Kaʿbah, when he touches the Black Stone, when he stands upon Safa and Marwah, at the standing at Arafah and Muzdalifah, and after stoning the first jamrah...
And the middle [prayer], and during his supplication after finishing the tasbīḥ following the prayers.

And when he finishes the two prostrations of the second rakʿah, he spreads out his left foot and sits upon it, erects his right foot, directs its toes toward the qiblah, places his hands on his thighs and spreads his fingers; the woman, however, sits on her hips (tawarruk).

He recites the tashahhud of Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him), pointing with the index finger at the testification, raising it at the negation and lowering it at the affirmation; and he does not add anything beyond the tashahhud in the first sitting, which is: "All greetings are for Allah, and prayers and good things; peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings; peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah; I bear witness that there is no deity except Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and messenger."

He recites al-Fātiḥah in what follows after the first two rakʿahs; then he sits and recites the tashahhud, then sends prayers upon the Prophet (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him), then supplicates with what resembles the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and then gives the salām to the right and the left, saying: "Peace and the mercy of Allah be upon you," intending those who are with him, as previously mentioned.
It is more excellent than the adhān.
Prayer in congregation is an emphasized sunnah for free men who are able to perform it without an excuse.
The conditions for the validity of the imamate for healthy men are six things:
[1] Islam,
And puberty,
And sanity,
And being male,
And recitation,
And freedom from excuses—such as nosebleed, stammering, lisping, and speech impediment—and lacking a condition such as purity and covering the nakedness.
The conditions for the validity of following [an imam] are fourteen things:
The follower's intention to follow [the imam], concurrent with his opening takbir,
And the man's intention to be an imam is a condition for the validity of women's following him,
And the imam being ahead of the follower by his heel,
And that he [the imam] not be of a lower state than the follower,
And he not be praying an obligation other than [the follower's] obligation,
And [the imam] not be a resident [leading] a traveler after the time [has expired] in a four-rakʿah prayer,
And not one who joined late,
And that no row of women separate between the imam and the follower,
And no river in which a boat passes,
And no road on which a cart passes,
And that no wall be between them by which knowledge of the imam's movements becomes uncertain; if it is not uncertain due to hearing or seeing, the following is valid according to the sound view.
And that the imam not be riding while the follower is on foot, or riding on a mount other than that of his imam.
And that he not be in one boat while the imam is in another that is not joined to it.
And that the follower not know of anything in his imam's state which invalidates [the prayer] in the follower's view—such as the issuance of blood or vomit after which he did not renew his ablution.

And valid is the following of one with wudu behind one performing tayammum, one who washes behind one who wipes, one standing behind one seated and behind a hunchback, one gesturing behind one like himself, and one praying a supererogatory prayer behind one praying an obligatory prayer.

And if the invalidity of his imam's prayer becomes apparent, he repeats; and it is incumbent upon the imam to inform the congregation to repeat their prayer to the extent possible, according to the preferred view.
Attendance of the congregation is dropped by any one of eighteen things:
Rain,
and cold (or hail),
and fear,
and darkness,
and imprisonment,
and blindness,
and paralysis,
and amputation,
and illness,
and being bedridden,
and mud,
and chronic disability,
and old age,
and the repeated study of fiqh with a group which he would otherwise miss,
and the presence of food for which his soul yearns,
and intending to travel,
and his attending to a sick person,
and severity of wind at night, but not during the day.
And if he is kept from the congregation due to one of its valid excuses, and his intention was to attend it had it not been for the excuse, he still obtains its reward.

blocks.ar: فَصْلٌ فِي ٱلْأَحَقِّ بِٱلْإِمَامَةِ، وَتَرْتِيبِ ٱلصُّفُوفِ
blocks.en: Section: On who is most entitled to lead the prayer, and the arrangement of the rows

blocks.translation: If there is among those present neither the owner of the house, nor someone with an appointed post, nor a person of authority, then the most knowledgeable is most entitled to lead the prayer, then the best reciter, then the most pious, then the eldest, then the one of best character,

Then the most handsome in face, then the most noble in lineage, then the one with the most pleasant voice, then the one with the cleanest garment; if they are equal lots are drawn, or the choice goes to the congregation, and if they differ the determining factor is what the majority chooses.
And if they put forward someone other than the most worthy, they have done wrong.

Disliked also is the imamate of the slave, the blind, the bedouin, the child of fornication, the ignorant, the sinner, the innovator; and prolonging the prayer, the congregation of the naked, and the congregation of women — but if they do so, the (female) imam stands in their midst, just as the naked do.
A single follower stands to the right of the imam, while more than one stand behind him.
The men are arranged in the first row, then the boys, then the hermaphrodites, then the women.

blocks.ar: فِيمَا يَفْعَلُهُ ٱلْمُقْتَدِي بَعْدَ فَرَاغِ إِمَامِهِ مِنْ وَاجِبٍ وَغَيْرِهِ
blocks.en: On what the follower does after his imam finishes a wajib act or other than it

blocks.translation: If the imam gives the salam before the follower has finished the tashahhud, the follower completes it.
And if the imam raises his head before the follower has said the tasbih three times in ruku' or sujud, he follows him.

If the imam adds an extra prostration, or stands after the final sitting forgetfully, the follower does not follow him but rather waits; then if the imam returns before fixing the additional prostration by an extra sajdah, the follower gives the salam with him.
But if the imam fixes (the extra act with a sajdah), the follower gives the salam by himself.

And if the imam stands before the final sitting forgetfully, the follower waits for him; if the follower gives the salam before his imam fixes the additional act with a sajdah, his fard prayer becomes invalid.
And it is disliked for the follower to give the salam after the imam's tashahhud but before the imam's salam.

blocks.ar: فَصْلٌ في ٱلْأَذْكَارِ ٱلْوَارِدَةِ بَعْدَ ٱلْفَرْضِ
blocks.en: Section: On the Remembrances Reported After the Obligatory Prayer

blocks.translation: Standing for the sunnah prayer immediately connected to the obligatory prayer is sunnah.
From Shams al-A'imma al-Halwani: there is no harm in reciting the regular litanies between the obligatory and the sunnah prayer.
It is recommended for the imam, after his salam, to shift toward his left side for the voluntary prayer that follows the obligatory, and to then face the people.
They seek Allah's forgiveness three times and recite Ayat al-Kursi and the Mu'awwidhat.

They glorify Allah thirty-three times, praise Him likewise, and magnify Him likewise, then they say: 'There is no deity except Allah, alone with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs the praise, and He is over all things capable.'
Then they supplicate for themselves and for the Muslims, raising their hands, and then wipe their faces with them at the end of it.
They are sixty-eight things:
[1] Speaking — even if inadvertently or by mistake;
[2] Supplicating with what resembles our ordinary speech;
[3] Giving salam with the intention of greeting — even inadvertently;
[4] Returning the salam with one's tongue;
Or by shaking hands,
And much action,
And turning the chest away from the qibla,
And eating anything from outside his mouth — even if little —,
And eating what is between his teeth if it is much — namely the size of a chickpea,
And drinking it,
And clearing the throat without excuse,
And saying 'uff',
And moaning,
And sighing 'aah',
And raising his weeping due to pain or calamity — not from remembrance of paradise or hellfire —,
And blessing a sneezer by saying 'yarḥamuka Allāh',
And answering an inquirer about a rival by saying 'lā ilāha illā Allāh',
And replying to bad news with the istirjāʿ (innā lillāhi wa innā ilayhi rājiʿūn),
And replying to pleasing news with 'al-ḥamdu lillāh',
And replying to something amazing with 'subḥān Allāh',
Or 'lā ilāha illā Allāh',
And anything by which he intends to give an answer — such as 'O Yaḥyā, take the Book' —,
And the sight of water by one who has performed tayammum,
And the expiry of the period for one wiping over leather socks,
And the removal of it (the leather sock),
And the illiterate person learning a verse,
And the naked person finding a covering,
And the ability of one praying by gesture to perform bowing and prostration,
And one obligated to observe order remembering a missed prayer,
And appointing as successor someone unfit to lead the prayer,
And the rising of the sun during the fajr prayer,
And the sun's passing the zenith during the Eid prayer,
And the entry of the time of Asr during the Friday prayer,
And the falling off of a splint due to healing,
And the cessation of the excuse of the legally excused person,
And intentionally breaking wudu,
Or by the act of someone other than him,
And fainting,
And insanity,
And major ritual impurity occurring through a look,
Or a wet-dream,

And the standing of a desirable woman in line with him in an unrestricted, shared prayer at the opening takbir, in a single location, without a barrier, while he did not gesture to her to move back, and he intended to lead her in prayer;
And the exposure of the nakedness of one who was overtaken by ritual impurity, even if he was forced to it — such as a woman uncovering her forearm for ablution;
And his recitation while going,
Or returning for ablution;
And his remaining for the length of performing a pillar after the occurrence of ritual impurity while awake;
And his passing by water nearby for some other purpose;
And his exiting from the mosque due to supposing that ritual impurity occurred;
And his crossing over the rows in a place other than the mosque due to his supposition (of ḥadath);
And his departing while supposing that he is not in ablution;
Or that the period of his wiping (over the khuffs) has expired;
Or that there is a missed prayer upon him;
Or an impurity — even if he did not exit from the mosque;
And his prompting (in recitation) someone other than his own imam;
And uttering the takbir with the intention of transferring to a prayer other than the one he is in;
(All of these invalidate the prayer) when these mentioned matters occur before the final sitting for the duration of the tashahhud.
And the following also invalidate it:
Lengthening the hamza in the takbir,
Reciting from a mushaf what he has not memorized,
Performing a pillar, or the possibility of doing so, while the awra is exposed,
Or with an impurity that prevents (the prayer's validity),
The follower preceding his imam in a pillar in which the imam did not share with him,
The latecomer following the imam in the prostration of forgetfulness,
Not repeating the final sitting after performing a spinal prostration he remembered after the sitting,
Not repeating a pillar that he performed while asleep,
The loud laughter of the imam of the latecomer,
His intentional ritual nullification after the final sitting,
Giving the salam at the end of two rak'as in a prayer that is not a two-rak'a prayer, thinking he is a traveler,
Or that it is the Jumu'a prayer,
Or that it is the Tarawih while it is actually the Isha,
Or he was newly converted to Islam and thought the obligatory prayer was only two rak'as.

If the worshipper looks at something written and understands it, or eats what is between his teeth — being less than a chickpea — without much action, or a passer-by passes in front of his place of prostration, the prayer is not invalidated, even though the passer-by has sinned.
Nor is it invalidated by his looking with desire at the private part of his divorced wife, according to the preferred view, even though revocation of the divorce is established thereby.
Seventy-seven things are disliked for the one who is praying:
[1] omitting an obligatory act,
[2] or a sunnah intentionally,
[3] his tucking up his garment,
[4] and his body,
[5] and turning over pebbles — except once to make the place of prostration even —,
[6] and cracking the fingers,
[7] and interlacing them,
[8] and placing the hands on the hips,
[9] and turning his neck,
[10] and squatting (al-iqʿāʾ),
And spreading his forearms (on the ground in prostration),
And rolling up his two sleeves away from them (the forearms),
And his praying in trousers (alone) while being able to wear a shirt,
And returning the salām by a gesture,
And sitting cross-legged without an excuse,
And tying up his hair,
And the i'tijār, which is binding the head with a kerchief while leaving its middle uncovered,
And tucking up his garment,
And letting it hang loose,
And wrapping himself in it such that he cannot bring out his hands,
And placing the garment under his right armpit and throwing its two sides over his left shoulder,
And reciting in a state other than standing,
And lengthening the first rak'ah in voluntary prayer,
And lengthening the second (rak'ah) over the first in all the prayers,
And repeating the same sūrah in a single rak'ah of the obligatory prayer,
And reciting a sūrah (placed in the Qur'an) above the one he already recited,
And separating with a sūrah between two sūrahs which he recited in two rak'ahs,
And smelling perfume,
And his fanning himself with his garment,
Or with a fan, once or twice,
And turning the fingers of his hands or his feet away from the qibla during prostration
and other than it,
And omitting placing the two hands upon the two knees during the bowing,
And yawning,
And closing his two eyes,
And raising them to the sky,
And stretching,
And minor (extraneous) action,
And taking a louse and killing it,
And covering his nose
and his mouth,
And placing something in his mouth that prevents the sunnah recitation,
And prostrating upon the fold of his turban,
And upon an image,
And confining (prostration) to the forehead without an excuse, omitting the nose,
And praying in the road,
And the bathhouse,
And the lavatory,
And the graveyard,
And on another's land without his consent,
And near to filth,
And while suppressing one of the two impurities (urine or stool),
Or wind,
And with a filth that does not prevent (the validity of the prayer) — unless he fears missing the time or the congregation; otherwise it is recommended to break it —,
And praying in work-clothes,
And with the head uncovered — not for the sake of humility —,
And in the presence of food to which he is inclined,
And anything that occupies the mind,
And impairs the reverence (khushūʿ),
And counting the verses,
And counting the tasbīḥ with the hand,
And the imam's standing inside the miḥrāb,
Or upon a raised platform;
Or on the ground alone;
And standing behind a row in which there is a gap;
And wearing a garment which has images on it;
And that there be (an image) above his head;
Or behind him;
Or in front of him;
Or alongside him there is an image — unless it be small, or with its head severed, or of something without a soul;
And that there be in front of him an oven;
Or a brazier with embers in it;
Or sleeping people;
And wiping dust from the forehead, when it does not harm him, in the midst of the prayer;

And designating a specific sura which he recites to the exclusion of others — unless for ease upon him, or for seeking blessing through the recitation of the Prophet (Allah bless him and grant him peace);
And neglecting to set up a sutra (screen) in a place where one expects someone to pass in front of the worshipper.

It is recommended to perform Fajr in daylight for men; to delay Zuhr for coolness in summer and to hasten it in winter—except on a cloudy day, when it is delayed; to delay Asr so long as the sun has not changed and to hasten it on a cloudy day; to hasten Maghrib except on a cloudy day, when it is delayed; and to delay Isha until a third of the night and to hasten it on a cloudy day.
And it is recommended to delay the Witr until the end of the night for one who is confident of waking up.
There are three times in which none of the obligatory or required prayers that became binding upon one's responsibility before their entry are valid:
[1] At the rising of the sun until it has risen high,
[2] and at its zenith until it declines,
[3] and at its yellowing until it sets.

The performance of what becomes obligatory during them is valid, though disliked—such as a funeral that presents itself and a verse of prostration recited in them—just as the Asr prayer of that very day at sunset is valid, albeit disliked.
In these three times, supererogatory prayer is disliked with a dislikedness amounting to prohibition, even if there is a cause for it, such as a vowed prayer and the two rak'ahs of tawaf.

blocks.ar: فِي اتِّخَاذِ السُّتْرَةِ وَدَفْعِ الْمَارِّ بَيْنَ يَدَيِ الْمُصَلِّي
blocks.en: On taking a sutrah and repelling the one passing in front of the praying person

blocks.translation: If he supposes someone will pass in front of him, it is recommended that he plant a sutrah at least a cubit long and as thick as a finger; the sunnah is that he be close to it and place it in line with one of his eyebrows, not facing it directly.
If he finds nothing to set up, let him draw a line lengthwise; though they also said crosswise, like a crescent.
What is recommended is to leave off repelling the one passing; repelling him by gesture or by saying subḥān Allāh is permitted, while combining the two is disliked.

He repels him by raising his voice in the recitation; and the woman repels him by gesturing or clapping the back of the fingers of her right hand upon the surface of her left palm, and she does not raise her voice because that is a fitnah.

He does not fight the one passing; what has been narrated concerning that is interpreted to mean that it was at a time when extraneous action in prayer was permissible, and that ruling has been abrogated.

blocks.en: On what is not disliked for the one praying

blocks.translation: It is not disliked to tighten the waist-sash, nor to gird oneself with a sword or the like provided one is not preoccupied with its movement; nor to refrain from inserting one's hands into a farajiyyah or a shiqqah according to the preferred opinion; nor to face a mushaf, a hanging sword, the back of a seated person who is conversing, a candle, or a lamp, according to the sound opinion.

Prostration on a carpet containing images is permitted provided he does not prostrate on the images themselves; and killing a snake or scorpion whose harm he fears, even by multiple strikes and even with turning away from the qibla, is permitted according to the more apparent view.

There is no harm in shaking off his garment so that it does not stick to his body during the bowing; nor in wiping his forehead of dust or grass after finishing the prayer, and even before finishing if it harms and distracts him from the prayer; nor in looking with the corners of his eyes without turning the face.
There is no harm in praying on bedding, carpets, and felts, though the best is prayer upon the ground or upon what it produces.
There is no harm in repeating the same sura in both rakʿahs of a supererogatory prayer.

blocks.ar: فِيمَا يُوجِبُ قَطْعَ ٱلصَّلَاةِ وَمَا يُجِيزُهُ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ
blocks.en: On what obligates breaking the prayer, what permits it, and other matters

blocks.translation: It is obligatory to break the prayer in response to the distress call of someone seeking aid from the worshipper, but not for the call of one of his parents.

It is permitted to break it on account of the theft of something worth a dirham, even if belonging to someone else, the fear of a wolf attacking sheep, or the fear of a blind person falling into a well or the like.

If the midwife fears for the death of the child, there is no harm in her delaying the prayer and attending to the child; and likewise the traveler, if he fears thieves and highway robbers, is permitted to delay the obligatory timed prayer.

One who deliberately abandons the prayer out of laziness is beaten severely until his blood flows, and is imprisoned until he prays it; the same applies to one who abandons the fast of Ramadan. He is not, however, killed unless he denies its obligation or treats it with contempt.
The witr is obligatory.
It consists of three rakʿahs with a single salutation.
He recites in each rakʿah of it al-Fatihah and a surah.
He sits at the end of the first two rakʿahs and limits himself to the tashahhud.
He does not recite the opening supplication when standing for the third rakʿah.
When he finishes reciting the surah in it, he raises his hands level with his ears, then says the takbir and recites the qunut while standing before the rukuʿ, throughout the entire year.
Qunut is not recited in other than the witr.
The meaning of qunut is supplication.

It is that he says: "O Allah, we seek Your help and ask Your guidance and seek Your forgiveness and repent to You; we believe in You and rely upon You and praise You with all good; we thank You and do not disbelieve in You; we cast off and abandon whoever disobeys You. O Allah, You alone we worship, and to You we pray and prostrate; to You we strive and hasten; we hope for Your mercy and fear Your punishment—indeed, Your severe punishment will overtake the disbelievers. May Allah's blessings and peace be upon the Prophet and his family."
The follower recites the qunut just like the imam.
When the imam begins the supplication that follows what has been mentioned...
Abu Yusuf said: They follow him and recite it along with him.
Muhammad said: They do not recite along with him, but rather they say "amin."

The supplication is this: "O Allah, guide us, by Your favor, among those whom You have guided; grant us well-being among those to whom You have granted it; take us as allies among those You have taken as allies; bless for us what You have given; and protect us, O our Lord, from the evil of what You have decreed. Indeed, You decree and none decrees against You. Surely, he whom You befriend is not humiliated, nor is he whom You oppose honored. Blessed are You..."
...our Lord, and exalted are You; and may Allah send blessings upon our master Muhammad and his family and grant peace.

Whoever does not know the qunut well, let him say: "O Allah, forgive me" three times, or: "Our Lord, grant us good in this world and good in the hereafter and protect us from the punishment of the Fire," or: "O Lord, O Lord, O Lord."
When one follows an imam who recites the qunut in Fajr, he stands silently with him during his qunut according to the more apparent view, and lets his hands hang at his sides.

If he forgets the qunut in Witr and remembers it during the bowing or upon rising from it, he does not recite the qunut and performs the prostration of forgetfulness; and if he recites the qunut after raising his head from the bowing, he does not repeat the bowing, and he performs the prostration of forgetfulness due to the qunut leaving its original place.

If the imam bows before the follower finishes reciting the qunut, or before he has begun it and he fears missing the bowing, he follows his imam; and if the imam omits the qunut, the follower performs it if it is possible for him to join the imam in the bowing; otherwise, he follows him.
If he catches the imam in the bowing of the third rakʿah of Witr, he is considered to have caught the qunut, so he does not perform it in what he missed.

One prays Witr in congregation only in Ramadan, and praying it with the congregation in Ramadan is more virtuous than performing it alone at the end of the night according to the choice of Qadi Khan, who said: this is the correct view; while others have authenticated the opposite.

The emphasized sunnah prayers are: two rakʿahs before Fajr, two after Zuhr, two after Maghrib, two after ʿIshāʾ, four before Zuhr, four before Jumuʿah, and four after it, all performed with a single salām.
It is recommended to pray four rakʿahs before ʿAsr, four before ʿIshāʾ and after it, and six after Maghrib.

In the first sitting of the emphasized four-rakʿah sunnah one limits oneself to the tashahhud, and one does not recite the opening supplication in the third rakʿah, unlike the recommended (four-rakʿah) prayer.
When he prays a voluntary prayer of more than two rakʿahs and does not sit except at its end...
...it is valid by istiḥsān, since it becomes a single prayer in which the obligatory element is the final sitting.
Adding more than four rakʿahs with one salām in the day's voluntary prayer, or more than eight at night, is disliked.
The most preferred in both [day and night] is sets of four according to Abū Ḥanīfah, while according to the two companions the best at night is two-by-two, and that is what the fatwa is given upon.
Night prayer is more excellent than day prayer.
Lengthening the standing is more beloved than multiplying the prostrations.

blocks.ar: فَصْلٌ في تَحِيَّةِ ٱلْمَسْجِدِ وَصَلَاةِ ٱلضُّحَى وَإِحْيَاءِ ٱللَّيَالِي
blocks.en: Section: On the Greeting of the Mosque, the Ḍuḥā Prayer, and Reviving the Nights

blocks.translation: Greeting the mosque with two rakʿahs before sitting is sunnah; performing the obligatory prayer suffices in its place, as does any prayer he performs upon entering, even without the intention of the greeting.
Two rakʿahs are recommended after ablution before its water dries, and four or more in the forenoon prayer (Ḍuḥā).
Also recommended are the night prayer, the istikhārah prayer (seeking guidance), and the ḥājah prayer (of need).
It is also recommended to spend in worship the last ten nights of Ramadan, the two nights of the two ʿīds, the ten nights of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, and the night of mid-Shaʿbān.
It is disliked, however, to gather for spending any of these nights in worship in the mosques.

blocks.ar: فَصْلٌ فِي صَلَاةِ ٱلنَّفْلِ جَالِسًا وَٱلصَّلَاةِ عَلَى ٱلدَّابَّةِ
blocks.en: Section: On the supererogatory prayer performed sitting and praying upon a riding animal

blocks.translation: The supererogatory prayer may be performed sitting even with the ability to stand, but he receives only half the reward of one standing unless he has an excuse; and according to the preferred view he sits in the posture of one performing the tashahhud.
It is permitted, without any dislike according to the sound view, for him to complete it sitting after having begun it standing, just as starting it sitting is permitted.

He may perform supererogatory prayer while riding outside the town, gesturing toward whichever direction his mount faces; and if he dismounts he continues upon his prayer—not if he merely mounts—even if it is from the regular sunnahs.
It is reported from Abū Ḥanīfah—may Allah have mercy on him—that he should dismount for the sunnah of Fajr because it is more emphasized than other sunnahs.

It is permissible for one performing a supererogatory prayer to lean upon something if he is fatigued without any dislike; but if it is without an excuse, then according to the more apparent view it is disliked because of the breach of proper etiquette.
An impurity present on the riding animal does not invalidate the prayer performed upon it, even if it is on the saddle.
And the two stirrups — according to the more correct view.
And the prayer of one walking is not valid, by consensus.

blocks.ar: فِي صَلَاةِ ٱلْفَرْضِ وَٱلْوَاجِبِ عَلَى ٱلدَّابَّةِ
blocks.en: On performing the obligatory and required prayer on a mount

blocks.translation: The obligatory prayers are not valid upon a mount, nor the required prayers — such as witr, the vowed, and what one commenced as supererogatory then invalidated — nor the funeral prayer, nor a prostration whose verse was recited on the ground, except for a necessity, such as fear of a thief against his person, mount, or clothes if he were to dismount, fear of a wild beast, mud of the place, the mount's unruliness, or not finding someone to mount him due to his inability.
Prayer in a litter upon a mount is like prayer upon the mount itself, whether the mount is moving or standing still.
If he places beneath the litter a piece of wood such that its base rests upon the ground, it takes the status of the ground, so the obligatory prayer is valid in it while standing.
The obligatory prayer in a ship while it is moving, performed seated without an excuse, is valid according to Abu Hanifa, with bowing and prostration.
The two (Abu Yusuf and Muhammad) said it is not valid except for an excuse, and that is the more apparent view; an excuse is like dizziness of the head and inability to disembark.
It is not permissible in it by mere gesture, by agreement.
A ship moored in the deep of the sea while the wind moves it strongly is like a moving ship; otherwise…
It is like the stationary (ship) according to the most correct view.
And if it is tied to the shore, his praying while seated is not permitted by consensus.
If he prayed standing and some part of the ship was resting on the bed of the ground, the prayer is valid.
Otherwise, it is not valid according to the chosen view, except when disembarking is not possible for him.
The worshipper in the ship faces the qiblah at the commencement of the prayer, and whenever it turns away from the qiblah he turns toward it during the prayer until he completes it facing it.
The Tarawih is a sunnah for men and women.
Praying it in congregation is a sunnah of sufficiency (sunnah kifayah).
Its time is after the Isha prayer.
It is valid to advance the Witr before the Tarawih or to delay it until after them.
It is recommended to delay the Tarawih until the third or half of the night.
It is not disliked to delay it until after that according to the sound view.
It is twenty rak'ahs with ten taslims.
It is recommended to sit after every four rak'ahs for a period equal to them, and likewise between the fifth tarwihah and the Witr.
It is sunnah to complete the Qur'an in it once during the month according to the sound view.
If the people become weary of it, he should recite an amount that does not lead to driving them away, according to the chosen view.
He should not omit the salutation upon the Prophet (Allah bless him and grant him peace) in every tashahhud of it, even if the people grow weary, according to the chosen view.
He should not omit the Thana, nor the tasbih of ruku' and sujud.
He should not perform the supplication if the people grow weary.
The Tarawih prayer is not made up if missed, neither individually nor in congregation.

blocks.en: Chapter on Prayer Inside the Ka'bah

blocks.translation: Obligatory and supererogatory prayer is valid inside the Ka'bah, and likewise on its roof, even if he does not take a barrier; however it is disliked because of the breach of etiquette in being above it.
Whoever places his back toward a direction other than the face of his imam, inside or above the Ka'bah, his prayer is valid; but if he places his back toward the face of his imam, it is not valid.
It is valid to follow an imam who is inside the Ka'bah while one is outside it, provided the door is open.
If they form a circle around the Ka'bah while the imam is outside it, the prayer is valid except for one who is closer to the Ka'bah than the imam on the imam's side.
The minimum journey by which the rulings change is a travel of three days, reckoned by the shortest days of the year, at a moderate pace including rest stops.
The moderate pace is the pace of camels and the walking of feet on land, on mountainous terrain whatever is appropriate to it, and at sea a wind of moderate strength.

Whoever intends a journey—even if he is sinful in his journey—shortens the four-rak'ah obligatory prayer once he passes the houses of his place of residence and also passes whatever is connected to it of its outskirts; but if the outskirt is separated from the town by a field or the distance of a bowshot, then passing it is not required.
The outskirt is the area designated for the town's needs, such as the running of animals and the burial of the dead.
Three things are required for the validity of the intention of travel:
[1] Independence in the ruling (i.e., not being a follower).
[2] Having reached puberty.
[3] That the duration of the journey not be less than three days.

Thus he does not shorten: one who has not passed beyond the built-up area of his place of residence; or one who has passed but is a minor; or a follower whose leader has not intended travel — like a woman with her husband, a slave with his master, and a soldier with his commander; or one intending less than the three [days]. The intention of residence or travel is considered from the principal, not from the follower, if he knows the intention of the one followed, according to the most correct view.

Shortening is obligatory according to us: so if he completes the four-rak'ah prayer and performed the first sitting, it is valid but with dislike; otherwise it is not valid unless he intended residence when he stood for the third rak'ah.

He continues to shorten until he enters his city, or intends a residence of half a month in a town or village; and he shortens if he intends less than that, or did not intend [a stay] and remained for years.

The intention of residence is not valid in two towns if he has not specified spending the night in one of them, nor in an open desert by one who is not a tent-dweller, nor for our army in enemy territory, nor for us in our land while besieging rebels.

If a traveler follows a resident within the time [of the prayer], it is valid and he completes it as four; but after the time has elapsed, no. In the reverse case [resident following traveler], it is valid in both cases, and it is recommended for the imam to say: "Complete your prayer, for I am a traveler," and it is proper that he say that before commencing the prayer.
The resident does not recite in what he completes after his traveling imam has finished, according to the most correct view.
The missed prayer of travel and residence is made up as two rak'ahs and four respectively, and what is taken into account in this is the end of the time.
The original homeland is nullified only by another like it, while the homeland of residence is nullified by another like it, by travel, and by the original homeland.
The original homeland is the place where one was born, or where he married, or where he did not marry but intended to settle and not to depart from it.
The homeland of residence is a place where one intends to stay for half a month or more.
The verifying scholars did not consider the homeland of mere dwelling, which is a place where one intends to stay for less than half a month.
And Allah knows best.

blocks.en: Chapter on the Prayer of the Sick

blocks.translation: When standing entirely is impossible for the sick person, or it becomes difficult due to severe pain, or he fears an increase or prolongation of his illness, he prays seated with bowing and prostration, sitting in whatever manner he wishes according to the most correct view; otherwise, he stands to the extent he is able.

If bowing and prostration are also impossible, he prays seated by gesturing, making his gesture for prostration lower than his gesture for bowing; if he does not make it lower than the bowing gesture, it is not valid.
Nothing should be raised up to his face for him to prostrate upon; but if this is done and he lowers his head, it is valid, otherwise not.

If sitting too is difficult, he gestures while lying on his back or on his side—the first being preferable—and he places a pillow under his head so that his face is directed toward the qiblah and not toward the sky, and it is recommended that he raise his knees if...
He is able [to fold his legs] so as not to stretch them toward the qibla.

If gesturing also becomes impossible, the prayer is postponed for him so long as he is able to comprehend speech. He said in al-Hidaya: this is the sound view; and the author of al-Hidaya affirmed in al-Tajnis and al-Mazid that the make-up lapses when his inability to gesture lasts more than five prayers, even if he still understands the content of speech, and Qadikhan declared this sound, and the same is in al-Muhit, and Shaykh al-Islam and Fakhr al-Islam chose it. In al-Zahiriyya he said: this is the apparent narration and upon it is the fatwa; and in al-Khulasa: it is the chosen view, and it was authenticated in al-Yanabi' and al-Bada'i', and al-Walwaliji affirmed it — may Allah have mercy on them all. And he does not gesture with his eye, his heart, or his eyebrow.
If he is able to stand but unable to bow and prostrate, he prays sitting with gesturing.
If an illness befalls him [during the prayer], he completes it according to what he is able to do, even if by gesturing, according to the well-known view.
If he prayed sitting while bowing and prostrating, then recovered, he continues from where he was; but if he was [only] gesturing, he does not.
Whoever becomes insane or unconscious for five prayers makes them up; but if more than that, he does not.

blocks.en: On the Dropping of Prayer and Fasting

blocks.translation: If the sick person dies and was unable to pray even by gesturing, it is not obligatory upon him to bequeath [a fidya] for it, even if [the prayers were] few.
Likewise the fast: when the traveler or the sick person breaks it and dies before settling down or recovering [there is no bequest required].
He is obligated to make a bequest for whatever he was able to perform and which remained as a liability upon him.
His guardian gives out on his behalf, from one-third of what he left, for the fast of each day and for the prayer of each time — even the witr — half a sa' of wheat or its value.
And if he did not make a bequest but his guardian volunteered (the payment) on his behalf, it is valid.
It is not valid that he (the guardian) fast or pray on his behalf.

When what he bequeathed does not suffice for what was due upon him, that amount is paid to the poor man, and it falls from the deceased to that extent; then the poor man gifts it to the guardian, who takes possession of it; then the guardian pays it again to the poor man, and it falls to that extent; then the poor man gifts it to the guardian and he takes it; then the guardian pays it back to the poor man, and so on, until what was owed by the deceased of prayer and fasting is fully discharged.
It is permissible to give the fidya for prayers to a single person all at once, contrary to the expiation of an oath.
And Allah knows best.

blocks.en: Chapter on Making Up Missed Prayers

blocks.translation: Order between a missed prayer and the current prayer, and between the missed prayers themselves, is obligatory.
It lapses by one of three things:
[1] The narrowness of the preferred time, according to the most correct view,
[2] and forgetfulness,
[3] and when the missed prayers reach six (excluding witr) — though its order is required, it (the sixth) is not considered as lifting (the obligation of order).
The order does not return by their reducing back to a small number, nor by the missing of a recent prayer after six old missed ones — according to...
according to the most correct view in both cases.

If he prays an obligatory prayer while remembering a missed prayer—even if it be the witr—his obligation is invalidated in a suspended manner: if the time of the fifth prayer ends after he has prayed prayers following the missed one while remembering it, all of them are valid and are not nullified by making up the missed prayer afterwards. But if he makes up the missed prayer before the time of the fifth prayer ends, the obligatory status of what he prayed while remembering it before becomes void and becomes supererogatory.
When missed prayers become numerous, he needs to specify each prayer; but if he wishes to ease the matter for himself, he intends the first Zuhr owed by him or its last, for example.
Likewise the fasting of two Ramadans, according to one of two differing authentications; but if it is from a single Ramadan, he does not need to specify.
Whoever becomes Muslim in the land of war is excused for his ignorance of the religious laws.

blocks.en: Chapter on Catching the Obligatory Prayer

blocks.translation: If he begins an obligatory prayer alone and then the congregation is established, he cuts it off and follows the imam—provided he has not yet prostrated for what he began, or has prostrated but in other than a four-rakah prayer.

If he has already prostrated in a four-rakah prayer, he adds a second rakah and gives the salam so that the two rakahs become supererogatory for him, then he follows the imam as one performing the obligation. If he has prayed three, he completes it, then follows the imam as one performing a supererogatory prayer—except in Asr. If he stands for the third rakah of a four-rakah prayer and the congregation is established before his prostration, he cuts off while standing with a single salam, according to the most correct view.

If he was performing the sunnah of Jumuah and the khatib came out, or the sunnah of Zuhr and the obligatory prayer was established, he gives salam at the end of two rakahs—and this is the soundest view—then he makes up the sunnah after the obligatory prayer.

Whoever arrives while the imam is already in the obligatory prayer follows him and does not busy himself with the sunnah unless it would be missed along with the obligatory; he makes up the sunnah of zuhr within its time before its post-fard pair.
He has not prayed zuhr in congregation by catching only one rakʿah, but he has attained its merit; and there is a difference of opinion regarding one who catches three rakʿahs.
He may perform voluntary prayer before the obligatory if he is safe from the time elapsing; otherwise not.
Whoever finds his imam bowing, makes the takbir, and stands until the imam raises his head, has not caught that rakʿah.
If he bowed before his imam after the imam had recited enough for the prayer to be valid, and the imam joined him in the bow, it is valid; otherwise not.
It is disliked for him to leave a mosque in which the adhan has been called until he prays in it, unless he is one who establishes another congregation.

If he left after having prayed alone, it is not disliked, except when the congregation is established before his departure in zuhr or ʿisha — in which case he follows in them as a performer of voluntary prayer.
A prayer is not to be repeated after one of its kind has been prayed.
And Allah the Exalted knows best.

blocks.en: Chapter on the Prostration of Forgetfulness

blocks.translation: Two prostrations, with tashahhud and salam, are obligatory for the inadvertent omission of an obligatory act, even if such omission be repeated.
If he omitted it deliberately, he has sinned, and repetition of the prayer becomes required in order to mend its deficiency; and he does not prostrate in...
...the deliberate (act) for the prostration of forgetfulness — it is said: except in three cases:
[1] Omitting the first sitting,
[2] And delaying a prostration from the first rakʿah until the end of the prayer,
[3] And his deliberating intentionally until it distracted him from a pillar.

It is sunnah to perform the prostration of forgetfulness after the salam, and he suffices with one salam to his right according to the more correct view; if he prostrated before the salam, it is disliked (with tanzīhī dislike).

The prostration of forgetfulness falls (is dropped) by the rising of the sun after the salam in fajr, by its reddening in ʿasr, and by the occurrence of anything that prevents continuing (the prayer) after the salam.
It is obligatory upon the follower (to perform it) due to his imam's forgetfulness — not his own forgetfulness.
The latecomer prostrates with his imam, then stands to make up what he missed; and if he forgets in what he is making up, he prostrates for that as well.
Not so the lāḥiq (one who missed part of the prayer due to a cause).
The imam does not perform the prostration of forgetfulness in the Friday and the two ʿid prayers.

Whoever forgets the first sitting of the obligatory prayer returns to it as long as he has not become upright standing, according to the apparent narration, and that is the most correct view; while the follower is like the supererogatory worshiper — he returns even if he has fully stood up.

If he returned while being closer to the standing posture, he prostrates for forgetfulness; if he was closer to the sitting posture, no prostration is required upon him according to the most correct view.
If he returned after having fully stood upright, scholars differed in declaring authoritative which view holds concerning the invalidity of his prayer.

If he forgets the final sitting, he returns to it so long as he has not (yet) prostrated, and he prostrates for forgetfulness; but if he has (already) prostrated, his obligatory prayer becomes supererogatory, and he adds a sixth rakʿah if he wishes — even in ʿasr — and a fourth in...
(...as in the case of) Fajr, and there is no dislike in joining them according to the correct view, and he does not perform the prostration of forgetfulness according to the most correct view.

If he sat for the final sitting then stood up, he returns and makes salam without repeating the tashahhud; but if he had already prostrated (in the extra rak'ah), his obligatory prayer is not invalidated, and he joins another rak'ah to it so that the two additional rak'ahs become a supererogatory prayer for him, and he performs the prostration of forgetfulness.

If he performed the prostration of forgetfulness in a pair of rak'ahs of a voluntary prayer, he should not, as a recommendation, build another pair of rak'ahs on it; but if he does build on it, he repeats the prostration of forgetfulness according to the chosen view.

If someone upon whom a forgetfulness is due makes the salam and another person follows him in prayer, the following is valid if he performs the prostration of forgetfulness, otherwise it is not valid.
He performs the prostration of forgetfulness even if he gave salam intending to terminate the prayer, as long as he has not turned away from the qiblah or spoken.

If someone praying a four-rak'ah or three-rak'ah prayer imagined he had completed it and gave salam, then realized he had only prayed two rak'ahs, he completes it and performs the prostration of forgetfulness.

If his deliberation was prolonged and he did not give salam until he became certain, then if it lasted the duration of performing a pillar of prayer, the prostration of forgetfulness becomes obligatory upon him; otherwise it does not.

The prayer is invalidated by doubt concerning the number of its rak'ahs if this occurred before its completion, and provided it is the first time doubt has occurred to him, or the doubt is not habitual for him. But if he doubts after his salam, it is not taken into account unless he is certain of an omission.

If the doubt becomes frequent, he acts upon the preponderance of his supposition; but if no supposition predominates, he takes the lesser number, and sits after each rak'ah which he supposed to be the last of his prayer.

blocks.en: Chapter on the Prostration of Recitation

blocks.translation: Its cause is the recitation, [obligatory] upon the reciter and the listener according to the sound view.
It is obligatory in a non-immediate (relaxed) manner if he is not in the prayer; and delaying it is disliked with a dislike of refinement (tanzīhī).
It is obligatory upon whoever recites a verse [of prostration], even if in Persian.
Reciting the [pivotal] letter of the prostration along with a word before or after it from its verse is like [reciting] the whole verse, according to the sound view.
Its verses are fourteen verses:
In al-Aʿrāf,
and al-Raʿd,
and al-Naḥl,
and al-Isrāʾ,
and Maryam,
and the first [prostration] of al-Ḥajj,
and al-Furqān,
and al-Naml,
and al-Sajdah,
and Ṣād,
and Ḥā Mīm al-Sajdah (Fuṣṣilat),
And Surat An-Najm,
and Surat al-Inshiqaq,
and Surat Iqra' (al-'Alaq).

The prostration is obligatory upon whoever heard it, even if he did not intend to listen — except for the menstruating woman, the postpartum woman, and the imam and the one following him by hearing it from another follower. If they heard it from someone other than him they prostrate after the prayer; and if they prostrated within it, it does not suffice them, although their prayer is not invalidated according to the apparent narration.
It is also obligatory upon hearing the [verse] in Persian if he understood it, according to the reliable position.
The authentication has differed regarding whether it is obligatory by hearing it from a sleeping or insane person.
It is not obligatory by hearing it from a bird or an echo.

It is fulfilled by a bowing or a prostration during the prayer other than the bowing and prostration of the prayer itself; and the prayer's bowing suffices for it if he intended it, as does its prostration even without intention, provided the immediacy of the recitation has not been broken by more than two verses.

If he heard it from an imam but did not follow him, or followed him in a different rak'ah, he prostrates outside the prayer according to the most apparent view; if he joined the imam before the imam's prostration for it, he prostrates with him; and if he joined him after the imam had already prostrated it within its rak'ah, he is legally considered as having caught it, so he does not perform that prostration at all.
The prostration belonging to the prayer is not made up outside it.

If [the verse] was recited outside the prayer and he prostrated, then he repeated it within the prayer, he must perform another prostration; but if he did not prostrate the first time, one prostration suffices him according to the apparent narration, just like one who repeated it within a single sitting — not two sittings.
The gathering changes by moving away from it — even while weaving — and by moving from one branch to another, and by swimming in a river or large pool, according to the soundest view.

It does not change by the corners of a house or mosque, even if large; nor by the movement of a ship; nor by one or two rak'ahs, a drink, eating two morsels, walking two steps; nor by reclining, sitting, standing, mounting or dismounting in the place of his recitation; nor by the movement of his mount while he is praying.
The obligation is repeated upon the listener when his own gathering changes while the reciter's gathering remains the same, but not in the reverse case, according to the soundest view.
It is disliked to recite a sura while omitting its verse of prostration, but not the reverse; and it is recommended to add one or more verses to it.
It is recommended to conceal it from anyone not prepared for it.

It is recommended to stand and then prostrate for it; and the listener should not raise his head from it before its reciter; nor is the reciter commanded to step forward nor are the listeners commanded to form rows — rather, they prostrate however they are.
Required for its validity are the conditions of the prayer, except for the takbir of consecration.
Its manner is that one makes a single prostration between two takbirs — which are sunnah — without raising the hands, without tashahhud, and without salam.

The prostration of thanksgiving is disliked according to Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) — one is not rewarded for it and leaving it is preferable; but the two companions said: it is an act of devotion for which one is rewarded.
Its form is like that of the prostration of recitation.

blocks.en: An important benefit for repelling every distress:

blocks.translation: The imam al-Nasafi said in al-Kafi: Whoever recites all the verses of prostration in a single sitting and prostrates for each one of them, Allah will suffice him in whatever concerns him.
The Friday prayer is an individual obligation upon whoever fulfills seven conditions:
[1] being male,
[2] and being free,
[3] and residence in a city, or in what is included within the limit of residence in it according to the most correct view,
[4] and health,
[5] and safety from an oppressor,
[6] and soundness of the two eyes,
[7] and soundness of the two legs.
And seven things are required for its validity:
[1] the city or its outskirts,
[2] and the ruler or his deputy,
[3] The time of Zuhr: it is not valid before it, and it is invalidated by its expiry.
[4] The sermon before it, with the intention of it, in its time.
[5] The presence of at least one person to hear it, from those with whom Jumu'ah is validly held — even if only one — according to the sound view.
[6] And the general permission (for people to attend).

[7] The congregation: they are three men besides the imam — even if they be slaves, travelers, or sick. The condition is that they remain with the imam until he prostrates; so if they depart after his prostration, he completes it alone as Jumu'ah, but if they depart before his prostration, it is invalidated. It is not valid with a woman or a child along with two men. It is permitted for a slave or sick person to lead it.

The city (miṣr) is every place that has a mufti, an emir, and a judge who carries out the rulings and establishes the legal punishments, and whose buildings reach the extent of those of Mina according to the apparent narration; and if the judge or emir is himself a mufti, that suffices in place of enumerating them separately.
Jumu'ah at Mina during the Hajj season is permitted for the caliph or the emir of the Hijaz.
It is valid to limit the sermon to the likes of a single tasbīḥ or taḥmīd, though with dislike (karāha).

blocks.en: The Sunnahs of the Sermon are Eighteen Things:

blocks.translation: [1] Ritual purity.
[2] Covering the 'awrah.
And sitting on the pulpit before commencing the sermon.
And the call to prayer before him, like the iqama.
Then his standing — with the sword in his left hand, leaning upon it — in every town conquered by force, and without it in a town conquered by treaty.
And facing the people with his face.
And his beginning with the praise of Allah.
And extolling Him with that of which He is worthy.
And the two testimonies of faith.
And the invocation of blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.
And admonition and reminder.
And reciting a verse from the Qur'an.
And two sermons.
And sitting between the two sermons.
And repeating the praise, the eulogy, and the blessing upon the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) at the start of the second sermon.
And supplicating in it for the believing men and women by seeking forgiveness for them.
And that he make the people hear the sermon.
And that he shorten the two sermons to the length of a surah from the long mufassal.
Lengthening the sermon and omitting any of the sunnahs is disliked.
Hastening to the Friday prayer and abandoning trade at the first adhan is obligatory, according to the soundest view.
When the imam comes out, there is no prayer and no speech until he finishes his prayer.
It is disliked for the one attending the sermon to eat, drink, fidget, or look around; and he should neither return a greeting nor say 'yarhamuk Allah' to one who sneezes.
The preacher should not greet the people when he ascends the pulpit.
Leaving the city after the call to prayer is disliked, so long as he has not yet prayed.
Whoever is not obliged to perform the Friday prayer, if he performs it, it discharges his obligation for the time.

Whoever has no excuse, if he prays Zuhr before the Friday prayer it is forbidden; and if he then sets out for it while the imam is performing it, his Zuhr is nullified even if he does not catch the Friday prayer.
It is disliked for the excused person and the imprisoned to perform Zuhr in congregation in the city on the day of Jumu'ah.
Whoever catches the Friday prayer in the tashahhud or in the prostration of forgetfulness completes it as Jumu'ah.

The prayer of the two Eids is obligatory, according to the soundest view, upon whoever is obligated to perform the Friday prayer, with its same conditions except for the sermon — it remains valid without it, though with wrongdoing, just as if the sermon were delivered before the Eid prayer.
On Eid al-Fitr, thirteen things are recommended:
That he eat, and that what is eaten be dates in an odd number,
and that he perform ghusl,
and use the siwak,
and apply perfume,
and wear the best of his clothes,
and pay the Sadaqat al-Fitr if it is obligatory upon him,
and display joy and cheerfulness,
and giving abundant charity according to his capacity,
and tabakkur, which is to wake up swiftly,
and ibtikar, which is hastening to the prayer-place,
and praying Fajr in the mosque of his neighborhood,
Then he proceeds to the prayer-place walking, saying takbir silently, ceasing it when he reaches the prayer-place in one narration, and in another narration when he opens the prayer,
and he returns by another route.
Performing voluntary prayer before the Eid prayer is disliked, both at the prayer-place and at home; and after it, only at the prayer-place, according to the choice of the majority.
The time of validity of the Eid prayer extends from the sun's rising by the measure of a spear until its zenith.

The manner of its prayer is: he intends the Eid prayer, then pronounces the opening takbir, then recites the praise (thana'), then pronounces the additional takbirs three times, raising his hands in each one; then he seeks refuge, then says the basmala silently, then recites al-Fatiha, then a sura — and it is recommended that it be Sura al-A'la {Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High} — then he bows.

When he rises for the second (raka'a), he begins with the basmala, then al-Fatiha, then a sura — and it is recommended that it be Sura al-Ghashiya — then he pronounces the additional takbirs three times, raising his hands in them as in the first raka'a. This (procedure) is preferable to placing the additional takbirs of the second raka'a before the recitation; but if he places the takbirs before the recitation in it, it is still permissible.
Then he delivers two sermons after the prayer, teaching in them the rulings of Sadaqat al-Fitr.
Whoever misses the prayer with the imam does not make it up.
It may be deferred, due to an excuse, only until the following day.

The rulings of al-Adha are like those of al-Fitr, except that in al-Adha he delays eating until after the prayer, pronounces takbir aloud on the way, and teaches the rulings of the sacrifice and the takbir of Tashriq in the sermon. It may be deferred, due to an excuse, up to three days; and the (practice of) ta'rif is of no account.

The Tashriq takbir is obligatory once, immediately after every obligatory prayer performed in a commendable congregation, from after the dawn of Arafa until the 'asr of Eid, upon a resident imam in a city and upon whoever follows him — even if he be a traveler, slave, or female — according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. The two (Sahibayn) said: it is obligatory immediately after every obligatory prayer upon whoever prays it, even if alone, traveling, or a villager, until the 'asr of...
The fifth (day) from the day of Arafah; by this it is acted upon and upon it is the legal verdict (fatwa).
There is no harm in saying the takbir after the prayer of the two Eids.
The takbir is that he says: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar; la ilaha illa Allah, wa-Allahu akbar; Allahu akbar, wa-li-Llahi al-hamd."

Two rak'ahs in the form of the supererogatory prayer are established as sunnah for the (solar) eclipse, led by the imam of Jumu'ah or one appointed by the sultan, without adhan, iqamah, audible recitation, or sermon; rather it is announced: "As-salatu jami'ah" (the prayer is congregational).

It is sunnah to lengthen them, and to lengthen their bowing and prostration; then the imam supplicates while sitting facing the qiblah if he wishes, or standing facing the people — and the latter is better — and they say amen to his supplication until the sun's clearing (from eclipse) is complete.
If the imam is not present, they pray individually, as is done for the lunar eclipse, terrifying darkness in the daytime, severe wind, and panic.
For it (istisqa') there is a prayer, performed without congregation, and there is supplication and seeking forgiveness.

It is recommended to go out for it for three days, walking on foot, in worn, washed, or patched clothes, in a state of humility and modesty, showing reverence to Allah Most High, with heads lowered, putting forward...
The charity (is given) each day before their going out (to the prayer).
It is recommended to bring out the animals, the senior elders, and the children.
