In Mecca and Jerusalem they assemble in the mosque, and this is fitting also for the people of the city of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

The imam stands facing the qibla, raising his hands, while the people are seated facing the qibla, saying amen to his supplication: ‘O Allah, give us rain that succours, wholesome, pleasant, fertilizing, abundant, speedy without delay, covering, pouring, general, and lasting,’ and whatever resembles it, secretly and aloud.
There is no turning of the cloak in it.
A dhimmī shall not attend it.

blocks.en: Chapter on the Prayer of Fear

blocks.translation: It is permitted in the presence of an enemy or a beast of prey, and in fear of drowning or fire.

When the people are in conflict (with an enemy) during prayer behind a single imam, he divides them into two groups: one facing the enemy, while he prays with the other one rakʿa of a two-rakʿa prayer, or two rakʿas of a four-rakʿa prayer or Maghrib; then this group proceeds on foot to (face) the enemy, and the other comes and he prays with them what remains, and he gives the salām alone. Then they go to the enemy, then the first group returns and completes (the prayer) without recitation, gives the salām and proceeds; then the other group comes and prays what remains with recitation.
If the fear intensifies, they pray as riders individually, by gestures, toward whichever direction they are able.
It is not permitted without the presence of an enemy.
It is recommended to carry weapons during the prayer of fear.
If they do not contend over praying behind a single imam, then it is preferable for each group to pray with its own imam, just as in the state of security.
It is sunnah to turn the dying person toward the qiblah on his right side, and lying on the back is permitted, with his head raised slightly.
He is prompted with the mention of the shahadah in his presence without insistence, and he is not commanded to say it.
Prompting him in the grave is prescribed; it has been said: he is not prompted, and it has been said: it is neither commanded nor forbidden.
It is recommended for the relatives and neighbors of the dying person to enter upon him and to recite Surah Ya-Sin in his presence; some of the later scholars approved Surah ar-Ra'd.
There is a difference of opinion regarding removing the menstruating and postpartum woman from his presence.

When he dies, his jaws are tied up and his eyes closed, and the one closing them says: "In the name of Allah and upon the religion of the Messenger of Allah. O Allah, make his affair easy for him, ease for him what comes after, make him happy in meeting You, and make what he has gone to better than what he has left behind."
A piece of iron is placed on his belly so that it does not swell.
His hands are placed at his sides, and it is not permitted to place them on his chest.
It is disliked to recite the Quran near him until he is washed.
There is no harm in informing the people of his death.
His preparation is to be hastened, so he is placed as he died upon a bier that has been incensed an odd number of times.
He is placed however it happens, according to the soundest opinion.

His nakedness is covered, then he is stripped of his clothes and given wudu — unless he is a small child who does not comprehend prayer — without rinsing the mouth or snuffing water, unless he was in a state of major ritual impurity.
Water boiled with lote-leaves or potash is poured upon him, and if not, then plain water — which is pure water.
His head and beard are washed with marshmallow.
Then he is laid on his left side and washed until the water reaches that side of him which is next to the board.
Then on his right side likewise.
Then he is sat up leaning against [the washer], and his belly is gently wiped; whatever comes out is washed away, but his ghusl is not repeated.
Then he is dried with a cloth, the embalming perfume is placed on his head and beard, and camphor on the places of prostration.
Cotton is not used in the washing, according to the manifest narrations.
His nails and hair are not clipped, nor is his hair or beard combed.
The woman washes her husband, contrary to him [a man washing his wife]; just as the umm walad does not wash her master.
If a woman dies among men, they perform tayammum for her with a cloth, as in the reverse case.
If a mahram blood relative is found, he performs tayammum [for her] without a cloth.
Likewise the problematic hermaphrodite is given tayammum, according to the manifest narration.
It is permitted for both the man and the woman to wash a young boy or girl who has not yet reached the age at which they are desired.
There is no harm in kissing the deceased.
It is incumbent upon the man to prepare [the funeral of] his wife, even if he is in financial hardship, according to the soundest opinion.
Whoever has no wealth — his shroud is upon the one obliged to maintain him.
If none is found, then from the public treasury.
If it does not give, whether due to inability or injustice, then [the burden falls] upon the people; and whoever cannot himself afford the funeral provisions asks them for him.
The shroud of a man by sunnah is a shirt, a waist-wrapper and an outer wrap, from the kind of clothing he used to wear in his life; while the minimum sufficiency is a waist-wrapper and an outer wrap.
White cotton is preferred.
Each of the waist-wrapper and the outer wrap extends from the crown of the head to the foot.
No sleeve, gusset, or collar-opening is made for his shirt, nor are its edges hemmed.
The turban is disliked according to the soundest view.
The shroud is wrapped from his left side then over his right side, and it is tied if its unfastening is feared.
For a woman, according to the sunnah, a head-cover for her face and a cloth strip to bind her breasts are added.
In the sufficiency-shrouding, a head-cover is added.
Her hair is made into two braids upon her chest over the shirt, then the head-cover is placed over it under the outer wrap, then the breast-binding cloth over it.
The shrouds are fumigated with incense an odd number of times before he is wrapped in them.
The shroud of necessity is whatever can be found.
The funeral prayer over him is a communal obligation (farḍ kifāyah).
Its pillars are the takbirs and the standing.
Its conditions are six:
The Islam of the deceased;
and his ritual purity;
and his being placed in front of the imam;
and his presence, or the presence of the greater part of his body, or half of it together with his head;
and that the one performing the prayer not be mounted on a riding animal without an excuse;
[6] And the deceased being upon the ground; so if he is upon a riding-animal or upon the hands of people, it is not valid according to the chosen view except in the case of an excuse.
[1] The imam standing opposite the chest of the deceased, whether male or female.
[2] And the thanā' (praise) after the first takbīr.
[3] And the ṣalāh upon the Prophet (Allah bless him and grant him peace) after the second.

[4] And supplication for the deceased after the third (takbir); nothing specific is required, though if one supplicates with the transmitted wording it is better and more eloquent. Among such is what has been preserved from the Prophet's (peace be upon him) supplication: «O Allah, forgive him, have mercy on him, grant him wellness, pardon him, honor his lodging, widen his entrance, wash him with water, snow, and hail, cleanse him of sins as a white garment is cleansed of filth, replace for him a home better than his home, a family better than his family, and a spouse better than his spouse; admit him into Paradise and protect him from the punishment of the grave and the punishment of the Fire».
He gives the salām after the fourth (takbīr) without any supplication, according to the apparent narration.
He does not raise his hands except in the first takbīr.
And if the imam pronounces five takbīrs, he is not to be followed; rather, his salām is awaited, according to the chosen view.

One does not seek forgiveness for an insane person or a child; rather, one says: «O Allah, make him a forerunner for us, make him for us a reward and a treasure, and make him for us an intercessor whose intercession is accepted».

The ruler has the greatest right to lead his (the deceased's) funeral prayer, then his deputy, then the judge, then the imam of the quarter, then the guardian; and the one having precedence may give permission to another, but if someone else prays, he may repeat it if he wishes, while those who prayed with the other do not repeat it with him.

The one who possesses the authority of precedence in it (the funeral prayer) is more entitled than the one to whom the deceased bequeathed the praying over him, according to the position given as the fatwa.
If he was buried without the prayer being performed, it is prayed over his grave, even if he was not washed, so long as he has not decomposed.
When several biers are gathered, performing a separate prayer for each of them is preferable, and the most excellent is given precedence, then the next most excellent.

If he combines them and prays over them once, he arranges them in a single row lengthwise on the side facing the qiblah, so that the chest of each is in front of the imam, and he observes the order: he places the men closest to the imam, then the boys after them, then the hermaphrodites, then the women.
If they are buried in a single grave, they are placed in the reverse of this order.

Whoever finds the imam between two takbirs does not follow him; rather, he waits for the imam's next takbir and enters with him, accompanying him in his supplication, then makes up what he missed before the bier is lifted.
But the one who is present at the imam's opening takbir does not wait.
Whoever arrives after the fourth takbir and before the salam has missed the prayer, according to the correct view.
It is disliked to pray over him in a mosque in which the deceased is, or outside it while some of the people are inside the mosque, according to the chosen view.

Whoever cries out at birth is named, washed, and prayed over; if he does not cry out, he is — according to the preferred view — washed, wrapped in a cloth, and buried, but the funeral prayer is not performed for him — just as for a child taken captive along with one of his parents, unless one of them or the child himself embraces Islam, or neither parent was captured with him.
If a disbeliever has a Muslim relative, he washes him as one washes an impure rag, wraps him in a cloth, and casts him into a pit, or else hands him over to the people of his own religion.

The funeral prayer is not performed over a rebel, nor a highway robber killed in the act of warfare, nor a killer who strangles treacherously, nor an assaulter who attacks the city at night with weapons, nor one killed in tribal partisanship — even though they are washed.
One who kills himself is washed and prayed over, but the funeral prayer is not performed for one who intentionally kills one of his parents.

blocks.en: Section: On Carrying and Burying the Deceased

blocks.translation: It is sunnah for four men to carry the bier, and it is proper to carry it forty paces, beginning with its right front (which is the side toward the carrier's left) upon his right shoulder, then its right rear upon it, then its left front upon his left shoulder, then concluding with its left rear upon it.
It is recommended to walk quickly with it, but without trotting, which is a jolting that shakes the deceased.
Walking behind the bier is more virtuous than walking in front of it, just as the obligatory prayer is more virtuous than the supererogatory.
Raising the voice with dhikr is disliked, as is sitting down before the bier has been set down.
The grave is dug to half a man's height, or up to the chest — and if more is added, that is good —
A niche-grave (laḥd) is dug, and a trench-grave (shaqq) is not used except in soft ground.
The deceased is brought in from the side of the qibla, and the one placing him says: "In the name of Allah, and upon the religion of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace."
He is turned toward the qibla on his right side, the knot is untied, and unbaked brick and reeds are evened over him — while baked brick and wood are disliked; and her grave is veiled, not his.
The dirt is poured over it, the grave is mounded (hump-shaped), and it is not made flat-squared.
Building upon it for ornament is forbidden, and is disliked even when only for reinforcement after the burial.
There is no harm in inscribing upon it so that the trace does not vanish nor be desecrated.
Burying inside houses is disliked, since it is exclusive to the prophets (peace be upon them); and burial in paved vaults is also disliked.
There is no harm in burying more than one in a single grave out of necessity, and a barrier of dirt is placed between each two.
Whoever dies on a ship while the land is far off and harm is feared, he is washed, shrouded, prayed over, and then cast into the sea.
It is recommended to bury him in the cemeteries of the locality where he died or was killed.
If he is moved before burial the distance of a mile or two, there is no harm; moving him farther than that is disliked.
It is not permissible to move him after burial by consensus, unless the land was usurped or has been taken back through preemption.
If he is buried in a grave dug for someone else, the cost of the digging is owed, and he is not removed from it.

The grave is opened for a piece of property that fell into it, for a usurped shroud, and for wealth left with the deceased; but it is not opened merely because he was laid facing other than the qibla or on his left side.
Visiting graves is recommended for men, and for women according to the most correct view.

It is desirable to recite Surah Ya-Sin, because of what has come, that he (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever enters the graveyards and recites Ya-Sin, Allah will lighten [the punishment] from them on that day, and he will have good deeds equal to the number of those in them."
Sitting at the grave for recitation is not disliked, according to the preferred view.

Disliked is sitting upon graves for other than recitation, treading upon them, sleeping and relieving oneself upon them, and uprooting grass and trees from the graveyard; but there is no harm in uprooting what is dry from them.
The slain one dies at his appointed term, according to us, the people of the Sunnah.

The martyr is one whom the people of war, or rebels, or highway robbers, or thieves in his home at night—even with a blunt instrument—killed, or who was found on the battlefield bearing a trace (of injury), or whom a Muslim killed wrongfully and intentionally with a sharp weapon, provided he was a Muslim, of legal age, free of menstruation, postnatal bleeding, and major ritual impurity, and was not carried away alive after the battle ended.
He is shrouded in his blood and his clothes, and the funeral prayer is performed over him without ritual washing.
Removed from him is what is not suitable as a shroud—such as fur, padded garments, weapons, and armor—and his clothing may be added to or reduced,
And it is disliked to remove all of it.

He is washed if killed while being a child, insane, menstruating, in postnatal bleeding, or in a state of major ritual impurity; or if he was carried off wounded after the conclusion of the battle — such as by eating, drinking, sleeping, taking medicine, the time of a prayer passing while he was conscious, being moved from the battlefield (except out of fear of being trampled by the horses), making a bequest, selling, buying, or speaking much.
And if what was mentioned occurs before the conclusion of the battle, he is not thereby considered a murtathth (one carried off wounded).

And whoever is killed in the town, while it is not known that he was killed wrongfully with an iron weapon, or was killed by a prescribed legal penalty or in retaliation — he is washed and prayed over.
